title: Dhammas: the hindrances
hookLine: desire present, he knows; absent, he knows; how it arises, how it goes (MN 10)

lines: THE SNACK, THE LEAF BLOWER, THE FOG.
cards: Sit quietly for five minutes and the usual visitors tend to arrive. First, the snack you suddenly want. Then irritation at the neighbor's leaf blower.
Then a heavy, sleepy fog. Then a jittery itch to check your phone. And finally a little voice: is this even doing anything?
It's tempting to read them as proof of being bad at meditation. The Buddha named all five, and made knowing them part of the practice. Today: dhammas, the hindrances.

teach.b: The fourth foundation is called dhammas, a hard word here. It can mean teachings, or mental qualities, or the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize in experience.

teach.h: FIVE HINDRANCES THAT COVER THE MIND.
teach.b: The first pattern is the five hindrances, the nivaranas, things that cover over a clear mind. Sensual desire. Ill will.
Sloth and torpor, that heavy, dull fog. Restlessness and worry. And doubt.
For each one, the sutta gives the same five-part instruction.
If desire is present in you, know that it's present. If it's absent, know that it's absent. Know how desire that hasn't arisen comes to arise.
Know how arisen desire is let go of. And know how, once let go of, it doesn't come back. So the hindrances aren't enemies to fight or proof that you're failing.
They're patterns to study. When did the sleepiness come in? Right after lunch.
What lifted it? Opening the window. When did the doubt show up?

teach.h: A NATURALIST OF YOUR OWN MIND.
teach.b: You become a naturalist of your own mind, watching creatures arrive and leave.
Elsewhere the Buddha compares a mind free of the hindrances to someone out of debt, recovered from illness, released from prison, freed from slavery, and safely across a desert.
That's the text's own picture of their going.
But the first step is only this: it came, and it went.

how: Meditation teachers in a number of Buddhist traditions teach the five hindrances early, so that practitioners can recognize sensual desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt as passing states rather than personal failures.

o: faults in the mind to confess and feel sorry for
patterns of mind to recognize, such as the five hindrances
the duties a person owes, set by their place in life

games.q: match each hindrance to how it shows up.

s: having the hindrances means you're bad at meditation
the Buddha made knowing them part of the practice itself.
the sutta asks you to know a hindrance's absence as well as its presence
present, absent, arising, let go, and not returning.
the Buddha compares a mind free of hindrances to someone released from prison
also out of debt, recovered from illness, and safely across a desert.

games.q: ten minutes into a sit, doubt shows up: 'this is pointless.' what does the sutta ask?
o: get up; doubt means it's not working.
know it: doubt is present; watch how it arose and how it goes.
argue with the doubt until it's gone.
games.why: doubt is one of the five hindrances. the instruction is to know it, study how it comes and goes, not to obey it or fight it.

practice: Rest with the breath and wait for one of the five visitors: wanting, irritation, dullness, restlessness, or doubt. When one arrives, name it, wanting is here, and notice what it feels like without chasing it away.
If you catch the moment it fades, name that too: wanting is gone.

wordCard.voice: Dhammas, the hindrances. Desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt: known when present, known when absent, watched as they come and go.

orig.note: Pali nīvaraṇa: a hindrance, something that covers over a clear mind.

carryVoice: Your line: it came, it went. The visitors aren't failures; they're patterns to study. That's day two hundred sixty.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the five hindrances
